subject: maths
stem: Which number is "four thousand three hundred six"?
rationale: 4 thousands, 3 hundreds, 0 tens and 6 ones is 4,306. 4,360 puts the 6 in the tens place; 4,036 drops the hundreds.

subject: maths
stem: Which of these four numbers is the biggest?
rationale: All have 5 thousands, so compare the hundreds: 9 hundreds beat 0, leaving 5,909, 5,990 and 5,900. Then the tens: 9 tens is most, so 5,990.

subject: maths
stem: Which of these numbers is odd?
rationale: An odd number cannot be put into pairs with none left over; it ends in 1, 3, 5, 7 or 9. 27 ends in 7. The others end in 4, 0 and 8, so they are even.

subject: maths
stem: How many even numbers are there from 1 to 10?
rationale: The even numbers are 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10: five of them. Leaving out 10 gives 4.

subject: maths
stem: A roti is cut into 4 equal parts. Each part is called
rationale: When a whole is divided into four equal parts, each part is a quarter. Two equal parts would make halves.

subject: maths
stem: How many quarters make one whole?
rationale: A quarter is one of four equal parts, so four quarters make the whole. Two quarters make only a half.

subject: maths
stem: How many centimetres make 1 metre?
rationale: Laying a 1 cm length 100 times end to end makes 1 metre, so 1 m = 100 cm.

subject: maths
stem: Which of these shapes has no corners and no straight edges?
rationale: A sphere, like a ball, is curved all over, so it has no corners and no straight edges. A cube, a cuboid and a pyramid all have corners.

subject: maths
stem: A school has 345 girls and 278 boys. How many children are there in all?
rationale: Add: 345 + 278. Ones 5 + 8 = 13, carry 1; tens 4 + 7 + 1 = 12, carry 1; hundreds 3 + 2 + 1 = 6. So 623. Forgetting the carries gives 513.

subject: maths
stem: A ribbon is half a metre long. How many centimetres is that?
rationale: One metre is 100 cm, and half of 100 is 50, so half a metre is 50 cm.

subject: maths
stem: Which of these is the same as one half?
rationale: Two of the four equal parts cover half the whole, so two quarters are the same as one half. Four quarters make the whole.

subject: maths
stem: You look straight down at a round tin of biscuits from above. What shape do you see?
rationale: From the top you see only the round lid, a circle. From the side the same tin looks like a rectangle, which is the trap.

subject: maths
stem: Her cousin's school has 612 children. Her school has 178 children fewer. How many children are in her school?
rationale: 'Fewer' means taking away: 612 − 178 = 434. Adding the two numbers, 790, is the usual slip.

subject: maths
stem: How many straight edges does a cube have?
rationale: A cube has 4 edges round the top, 4 round the bottom and 4 joining them: 12. 6 is the number of faces and 8 the number of corners.

subject: maths
stem: Raju has an odd number of marbles. He gets one more marble. Is the number of marbles he has now odd or even?
rationale: An odd number has one left over when paired; one more marble pairs it up, so the new number is always even. It can be told without knowing the number.

subject: science
stem: Which body part does an elephant use to pick up food and drink water?
rationale: An elephant's long trunk picks up food and sucks up water. Tusks are teeth, and ears and tail are not used for eating.

subject: science
stem: A sparrow has a short, strong beak. It helps the sparrow to
rationale: A short, strong beak cracks seeds. A long thin beak sucks nectar, and a sharp curved beak tears meat.

subject: science
stem: An eagle catches its prey with its
rationale: An eagle grips its prey with sharp claws and tears it with its sharp, curved beak. Feathers and a tail help it fly, not catch.

subject: science
stem: Earthen pots used to store grain were lined inside with neem leaves. Why?

options.A: To keep insects away from the grain
options.B: To make the grain taste sweeter
options.D: To give the grain a green colour

rationale: Neem leaves keep insects and pests away, so the stored grain stays safe. They do not sweeten or colour it.

subject: science
stem: Natural dyes can be made from
rationale: Flowers, leaves, bark and roots such as marigold, hibiscus and beetroot give colours that can be made into natural dyes.

subject: science
stem: Which of these foods gives us the most energy?
rationale: Rice, wheat, potatoes and millets are energy-giving foods. Water and salt are needed by the body but give no energy.

subject: science
stem: Pulses, milk and eggs mainly help our body to
rationale: Pulses, milk, eggs and nuts are body-building foods: they help the body grow and repair itself.

subject: science
stem: Jowar, ragi and bajra are all
rationale: Jowar, ragi and bajra are millets, grains rich in nutrients. Pulses are dals such as moong and chana.

subject: science
stem: A meal with energy-giving, body-building and protective foods in the right amounts is called
rationale: Balanced food has all three kinds of food in the right amounts. A meal can be raw or sweet without being balanced.

subject: science
stem: A sunbird has a long, thin beak. It mainly uses it to
rationale: A long, thin beak reaches deep into flowers to drink nectar. Cracking nuts needs a short, strong beak.

subject: science
stem: Which of these mainly protects us from diseases?
rationale: Fruits and vegetables are protective foods that help keep diseases away. Sugar, honey, rice and wheat mainly give energy.

subject: science
stem: By looking at a bird's beak and claws, we can best guess
rationale: A bird's beak and claws suit the food it eats: a seed-cracking beak, a nectar-sipping beak, claws for catching prey. They tell little about its age or song.

subject: science
stem: Bees visit flowers to collect nectar, and many flowers need bees to make seeds. This shows that

options.A: bees harm the flowers they visit
options.B: flowers do not need any animals
options.C: bees eat only the leaves of plants
options.D: plants and animals depend on each other

rationale: Each helps the other: the bee gets food and the flower gets help to make seeds. This is the web of life, where plants and animals depend on each other.

subject: science
stem: Ravi eats only rice and potatoes every day. What is his food missing most?

options.C: Food that is cooked at home

rationale: Rice and potatoes are both energy-giving, so energy is the one thing he does get. He is missing body-building foods (pulses, milk) and protective foods (fruits, vegetables).

subject: science
stem: In the mud by a pond you see footprints with skin joining the toes. Which animal most likely made them?
rationale: Skin between the toes (webbed feet) helps a duck paddle in water, and it lives by ponds. A hen, dog and cat have separate toes.
